name: Side plank
angleNote: Height of the forearm support above the floor: 0 = on the floor, higher = forearm on a bench, the body tilted up. Front view of the body lying on its side. A hold: the slider compares set-ups.

strength.note: Isometric trunk side-bending with the trunk upright, men: 163 Nm (left 162, right 165; women 101–117 Nm); it falls as the trunk is already bent (140 Nm at 20°, 120 Nm at 30°). Seated with the hips strapped. Only the straight-trunk value is used.
strength.source: Kumar S, Dufresne RM, Van Schoor T (1995). Human trunk strength profile in lateral flexion and axial rotation. Spine 20(2):169–177. doi:10.1097/00007632-199501150-00007

strength.note: Isometric hip abduction, men aged 20–29: 185 Nm. The lower hip holds both legs (the upper leg lies on the lower one). The hip abduction exercise uses Neumann et al.'s 110 Nm from a mixed group of 40 adults; with that, the side plank's hip load would exceed the maximum, while Ekstrom et al. measured the gluteus medius at 74% of its maximum, so the young men's value is used here.
strength.source: Danneskiold-Samsøe B, Bartels EM, Bülow PM, Lund H, Stockmarr A, Holm CC, Wätjen I, Appleyard M, Bliddal H (2009). Isokinetic and isometric muscle strength in a healthy population with special reference to age and gender. Acta Physiol 197(Suppl 673):1–68 doi:10.1111/j.1748-1716.2009.02022.x

muscles.name: Obliques (lower side)
muscles.note: Hold the trunk straight against side-bending: the external oblique reached 69% of its maximum in the side bridge (Ekstrom et al.) and 99 ± 36% in Horsak et al.'s (the most of eight stabilisation exercises), against about 54% of the side-bending strength in this model. The internal oblique works with it: 52 ± 25% (Horsak et al.).
muscles.source: Ekstrom RA, Donatelli RA, Carp KC (2007). Electromyographic analysis of core trunk, hip, and thigh muscles during 9 rehabilitation exercises. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 37(12):754–762. doi:10.2519/jospt.2007.2471 (Tables 1, 3 and 4: 30 healthy adults, % of maximal isometric activation); Horsak B, Wunsch R, Bernhart P, Gorgas AM, Bichler R, Lampel K (2017). Trunk muscle activation levels during eight stabilization exercises used in the functional kinetics concept: a controlled laboratory study. J Back Musculoskelet Rehabil 30:497–508. doi:10.3233/BMR-140259 (abstract and discussion: 20 young adults, 14 women, right side, % of maximal isometric activation)

muscles.name: Back extensors (lower side)
muscles.note: Side-bend the trunk too: longissimus 40% and multifidus 42% of their maximum in the side bridge (Ekstrom et al.), far more than in the front plank (5–6%); the lumbar back muscles 52 ± 14% in Horsak et al.'s side bridge.
muscles.source: Ekstrom RA, Donatelli RA, Carp KC (2007). Electromyographic analysis of core trunk, hip, and thigh muscles during 9 rehabilitation exercises. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 37(12):754–762. doi:10.2519/jospt.2007.2471 (Tables 1, 3 and 4: 30 healthy adults, % of maximal isometric activation); Horsak B, Wunsch R, Bernhart P, Gorgas AM, Bichler R, Lampel K (2017). Trunk muscle activation levels during eight stabilization exercises used in the functional kinetics concept: a controlled laboratory study. J Back Musculoskelet Rehabil 30:497–508. doi:10.3233/BMR-140259 (abstract and discussion: 20 young adults, 14 women, right side, % of maximal isometric activation)

muscles.name: Rectus abdominis
muscles.note: 34% of its maximum in the side bridge (Ekstrom et al.), 28 ± 20% in Horsak et al.'s. With a maximal breath out it reached about 75% of maximum (Oliva-Lozano & Muyor's review).
muscles.source: Ekstrom RA, Donatelli RA, Carp KC (2007). Electromyographic analysis of core trunk, hip, and thigh muscles during 9 rehabilitation exercises. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 37(12):754–762. doi:10.2519/jospt.2007.2471 (Tables 1, 3 and 4: 30 healthy adults, % of maximal isometric activation); Horsak B, Wunsch R, Bernhart P, Gorgas AM, Bichler R, Lampel K (2017). Trunk muscle activation levels during eight stabilization exercises used in the functional kinetics concept: a controlled laboratory study. J Back Musculoskelet Rehabil 30:497–508. doi:10.3233/BMR-140259 (abstract and discussion: 20 young adults, 14 women, right side, % of maximal isometric activation); Oliva-Lozano JM, Muyor JM (2020). Core muscle activity during physical fitness exercises: a systematic review. Int J Environ Res Public Health 17(12):4306. doi:10.3390/ijerph17124306 (results summary, values of the primary studies as reported there)

muscles.name: Gluteus medius (lower side)
muscles.note: Holds the pelvis up on the lower leg: 74% of its maximum in the side bridge, the most of nine exercises (Ekstrom et al.), against about 54% of the hip abductors' strength in this model.
muscles.source: Ekstrom RA, Donatelli RA, Carp KC (2007). Electromyographic analysis of core trunk, hip, and thigh muscles during 9 rehabilitation exercises. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 37(12):754–762. doi:10.2519/jospt.2007.2471 (Tables 1, 3 and 4: 30 healthy adults, % of maximal isometric activation)

phases.name: Floor
phases.text: On the forearm on the floor: the body is almost horizontal sideways, the longest lever.

phases.name: Low bench
phases.text: The load falls with the cosine of the tilt.

phases.name: High bench
phases.text: Steeply inclined: a progression towards the full side plank.

variants.name: Side plank on the forearm
variants.notes: On one forearm (elbow under the shoulder) and the edge of the lower foot, body straight. The forearm carries about two thirds of the weight.

variants.name: Side plank from the knees
variants.notes: Knees bent, the lower knee on the floor: a shorter lever, much less load at the lower back and hip.

trunk3d.note: 3D view: the trunk muscles of the OpenSim lumbar spine model (Christophy et al. 2012, MIT licence) set on the body (the lumbar spine straight, as held), shaded by this exercise's muscle effort. Groups the exercise doesn't load stay grey. Lying on the left side, facing you.
